title: The Epicycles of Identity Politics
author: Geoff Shullenberger
content:
![The Epicycles of Identity
Politics](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-01-at-6.43.47
---AM.png)

One of the more revealing moments in what we now call "Woke 1" was the
firestorm around the philosophy professor Rebecca Tuvel's paper "In Defense of
Transracialism." Tuvel began by observing the contrasting progressive
reactions to the gender transition of Caitlyn Jenner, which was widely
celebrated, and the racial "transition" of Rachel Dolezal, which was just as
widely reviled. Given that Tuvel later became an anti-woke _cause c elebre_,
it is noteworthy that she presented her defense of Dolezal as an extension of
existing progressive assumptions about trans identity. "Since we should accept
transgender individuals' decisions to change sexes," she asserted, "we should
also accept transracial individuals' decisions to change races."

Despite the efforts of activists and some of her fellow academics, Tuvel's
paper was never retracted, but nor did her argument prevail; nearly ten years
later, the disjunction she pointed out persists. In the years since, prominent
figures in various fields and institutions have continued to face a backlash
when it was revealed that they had misrepresented their ethnic origins.
Meanwhile, in the same spaces, changing one's gender identity is more
commonplace and socially accepted than ever.

This divergence, as others have noted, bespeaks a selective application of
opposed conceptions of social reality. In the dominant progressive
understanding, gender and sexuality are the realm of what Judith Butler called
"performativity": As soon as individuals declare an identity, it assumes the
status of ultimate reality. But race and ethnicity don't work this way: A
statement about one's racial or ethnic identity must evidently correspond to
some pre-existing reality that can be externally verified. Thus, identity is
at once essential and fixed and malleable and constructed, depending on which
part of it you focus on.
